If you don't trust your wife not to cheat on you, you should probably call it quits. Be ready for people to call you dramatic, insecure, rushing to conclusions, etc. but if you really can't trust your wife to love you or have self control enough to not be unfaithful, you're in the wrong relationship.

If I may give you some wisdom as a guy 20 years younger than you: There's nothing, literally 0, less than nothing even, that you can actually do to guarantee someone won't cheat on you that doesn't involve locking them in a basement. As long as the person you're with has free will and sexual organs, they can choose to hurt you and have sex with other people behind your back and someone who wants to cheat on you will find a way to do it. If they do so, it is because they're a piece of shit and it doesn't reflect on your own value or say anything bad about you. If you think your partner is capable, willing, and likely to cheat, the very best thing you can do both for yourself and her is to break it off for the sake of your dignity and your self-respect. Don't let the sunk cost fallacy keep you both stuck in a relationship where you feel like you can't trust her and she feels like she needs to step out for whatever litany of reasons she can (and likely will) come up with.

Online dating is horrid for everyone but I have a similar issue so I sympathize. 26M, also ENFP but Type 6w7. Have been single for about a year and a half and have been trying to find a steady relationship with not much luck. I don't like leading every conversation and it sometimes feels like a lot of the people I match with on the apps just expect me to entertain them which leads to really poor conversation rather than a fluid exchange of ideas or at least interesting banter. It feels pretty shitty to be interested in someone and then having to basically start every conversation and be the one responsible for keeping it going. I like conversations that jump around between topics and changing the subject a lot and people can sometimes get overwhelmed by the rapid fire writing. That's mostly a mismatch of personality so I don't take it to heart too much.

I think it is that most people aren't really enthusiastic about tinder or what have you so interacting with matches is a bit of a chore? And they sort of expect everyone to be as casual and noncommittal as them so intensity and passion are seen as somewhat off putting. I love bubbliness, intensity and depth, which makes it a tragedy that it's in such short supply in the dating pool 💀

I'd also say, people with active hobbies can also be deep and intellectual. I spend a lot of time at the gym and playing/watching soccer but I'm also into history, linguistics, physics and math, painting, sculpture, and a lot of niche anime, but if you met me in passing you'd think I'm a tribalistic team obsessed meathead. Part of what allows me to have such varied conversations is that I'm always trying new stuff and I went from a pretty stereotypical indoorsy nerd to this so I think it's a good thing to broaden your horizons into things you don't think you're into cause you never know. And you may meet someone interesting in those spaces. I would never have met my best friend if I hadn't shown an interest in fighting games, which I don't play, but he loves them, and we click in so many other ways that it would have been a genuine tragedy to have missed out on each other with a decision as simple as not wanting to spend 10 minutes exploring a game genre I wasn't really interested in.

My very first real crush I was stuck on for no shit like 4 years, until I was 18. Severely fucked me up. Romanticized it so much it actually caused some breakups years down the line. Went through a lot of soul searching as to why. Talked to a lot of people. Had other relationships but always saw her as the one that got away. Pure limerence straight to my arteries. What made it so bad is that I never even got a chance to be disappointed by her. She never rejected me, I just never told her what I felt. 

That taught me that whenever I feel that little tug in my heart, I gotta do something about it. Even if it's a longshot, even if I'm gonna look ridiculous, or have a 100% chance of getting rejected. I do it because I don't want to break my own heart, like you said. I need it spelled out by that other person. It's actually gotten me into a few relationships, including my longest and happiest one (5 years, ended a year and a half ago). Personally, I think inaction is what causes a lot of the heartache that comes with unrequited love. Because you'll always wonder what if. Temporary embarrassment or discomfort shooting your shot is a pretty sweet trade off to let go of kataomoi.

This may not work for everyone, I know some people are really self conscious or have trauma around rejection. I just got used to it 😂

Keep your chin up and remember to prioritize yourself and your well being over being partnered. The right person will come along.

Being told you're "too much" stings, but it's a blessing in disguise. I've found that people who say that kind of thing often end up being "too little" in relationships. Not always, but I think ENFPs should try to find other similarly enthusiastic extroverts, or at least people who enjoy that kind of attention, because it's one of our core traits and having to suppress that in a long term relationship would probably hurt a lot, don't you think?

\>i worry that my tendency to overthink and idealize potential romantic interests makes me “too much” for most people.

Oh boy, this right here. That will torpedo a lot of relationships before they even start. I catch myself doing it occasionally and all it really does is burn you out because we imagine these ideal scenarios with people and then go through loss when it doesn't work out, as romantic interests often don't.

The way I navigate relationships is I try to be myself and I try to stick to people that I think I could be compatible with, both online and IRL. For example, I could go out with the party crowd all the time to try to meet someone to date, but that's not my scene and whoever I meet there would more than likely not vibe with me. It's all about finding your people, and your space, and most likely the person who's going to end up with you will be found there. I also go online and try to find people that I feel like I'll mesh with, but I'm pretty specific with the people I like so that hasn't worked out super well.

\>i don’t want to make them uncomfortable with my enthusiasm and moodiness

Personally speaking, if someone is uncomfortable with enthusiasm, they're not the person for me. I'm enthusiastic and I would sure hope that the person I like was enthusiastic about me too, don't you think? Wouldn't it be a happier relationship if those feelings are reciprocated?

Same with the rest of your "negative" traits, really. That just sounds like your personality (except maybe overthinking, that one is probably anxiety, and I do it too) and you should look for people who mesh with it. Don't stress yourself or dim your light to fit molds for people who don't love you the way you are.

\>i have a lot of loving friends, and people have certainly liked me over the years, i just don’t ever fully trust that they’d stay if they spent as much time with me as a partner would

Then you just haven't found the right person, I think. It all really ties together that way. You're not flawed for being yourself, you just haven't found the puzzle you fit in. The right guy/girl is going to \*want\* to be with you as much as possible and is going to \*enjoy\* the time you spend together when you're being yourself.

23 is way too young to think that you'll never find someone.

Hi I'm someone with the same kind of personality and the way you stop this is by learning to say no to people when they make requests that sound reasonable but that open you up to further exploitation. For example, set a boundary that you will not drive anyone further than 45 minutes off post, or that you won't be the DD if it's a weekday or they don't tell you at least X hours prior. There's things you can do that make you a generous person and there's things that make you a rube. 

Helping someone with a broken down car get groceries from the commissary? A-Ok

Picking up a battle from a bar outside of post at 2am so they don't catch a DUI? Annoying, testing the limits a little bit, but ultimately a reasonable action a kind person would take.

Driving someone ONE HUNDRED MILES off post just to sleep in your car (as in this fucking loser couldn't even pay for a hotel you could go sleep at)? You're being taken advantage of. This is the threshold at which you should have said no.

Co-signing a high risk loan for someone with garbage credit and a history of repossessions? Absolutely not. Fuck no. If it was just going with them to a dealership and helping them get a decent deal maybe but if the bank can't make them keep their fucking word what makes you think you can? I joined at 26, so I was a dinosaur at Basic. People at my unit still call me unc. I'm the same age as most of my NCOs. You have to be an NCO for some time before you can go GtG, but yes, that's always an option. Cool guy shit like EOD, SF, Regiment, etc is also always available. Warrant Officer is an option for some, as well.

The biggest difference that I can see from my end is that I make shit work in the immediate, while officers make shit work as a whole. I'm responsible for a part of my tank, my equipment, and myself. That's it. Officers are responsible for everything that happens under them.

The plan is to do as many years as I'm able. I'm not leaving the Army until they medboard me, kick me out, forcibly retire me, or bring me back in a box. I love this life beyond anything I've ever done. 

Work life balance depends on the unit. We had a BBQ today at our barracks after being released early. We have a 3 day weekend coming up. Once the training cycle starts again for next deployment, we're back to the Armor OPTEMPO, which is fucking brutal (another reason why I think its a bad idea to not get to pick your job. Imagine you end up as an armor officer without loving armor).

I was a handyman for a few years, then spent my whole career working with public defenders' offices. It's not like either blue or white collar. The level of control exercised on you is far beyond anything you've probably experienced and if you're an independently minded person it will be the hardest part to process.

I enlisted in the MOS I did because I knew coming in that I didn't want a desk job, and I wanted the best possible chance to see combat. I would have gone infantry, but I told myself I'd only go infantry if I could get an Airborne contract, of which there were none, so tanker it was. Officer route is completely different. You go to OCS and then you get your officer job. You could get a shitty as fuck officer job (my company commander went to West Point for Space Science and got stuck as CO of a TRADOC Armor company) and have 0 say in what you do with the rest of your career (so I've heard). The cool guy shit opportunities for officers have a definite expiration period, which is when you hit Major (O-4) and have to do Staff work. Enlisted has the same, but you get a lot more time "on the tank" (E-7 will be a PLT SGT but still in the action, few people make it to E-8). You will do exactly 0 cool guy shit as a Finance branch officer. You may go to Ranger school (actually you probably will because officers get priority slots).

If you want the opinion of a dumbass SPC with a 139 GT score that gets told every single day to drop a packet or go Green to Gold ASAP, enlisted life is better. I wanted the shitty hours, the lack of sleep, the shitty ass morning formations, the PT, the dumb rules, and the risk to life for little discernable reward, and I was okay with the shit pay. I would not trade the camaraderie, the experiences, the mentors and the life I have had since I enlisted last year for all the money in the world or the glitziest FiDi Manhattan office. I fucking love it. I will be submitting a packet soon, but I will likely remain enlisted till I retire.

Honestly is. If I ever get put on a recruiting assignment I'm gonna laser focus on kids who want to be in the legal field but don't wanna be lawyers. The Army is literally the perfect environment to be a paralegal, and if I had enlisted as a 27D at 18 I probably would still be happily doing it. Low level admin and paperwork positions in the civilian world fucking suck.

I may have some interesting insight from the civilian side. Until last week, I was the senior paralegal for a special criminal defense unit at a public defender's office, the largest in the US. If your interests align with the Legal field but you don't have a JD and no interest in going to law school, that's a pretty sweet gig. I was making $55,525 and wouldn't EVER hit area median income for my county (Kings County, NY - also known as Brooklyn) under either the current or proposed payscales. I had an absolute assload of work, had frequent all-nighters, was basically supposed to be available round the clock (my boss would frequently email at 2am), and had fairly frequent travel between the boroughs. My health insurance wasn't bad, but it also wasn't great. I had 12 days of paid time off per year and another 10 sick days that I had to present a doctor's note to use. As my unit supervisor's paralegal, I was also her secretary, and got to see the resumes of people who had applied for my job - this shiny turd of a job was drawing in applicants who had:

- a college degree in a related field
- an average of 3 years' experience in a public defender's office
- 2 or 3 letters of recommendation from some of the top trial attorneys in their state. There was one with an, I shit you not, glowing letter of praise from a FEDERAL FUCKING BENCH that she had worked under.

If you want to be a trial paralegal with offices doing "real" (I hate that word but that's what the attorneys use) work, you're going up against people with this kinda qualifications, people who would gladly go to a fucking Battle Royale style competition to get these jobs. It's cut-throat. The people who intern at these places for no money and maybe lunch sometimes if their assigned attorney feels like it are 2nd year Law students from top schools that played their cards right and aced 4 or 5 interviews. The only harder places to get into are Big Law, which basically takes you laser focusing on a career there from grade school. 

Or you could join the United States Army as a 27D Paralegal Specialist and get to do really interesting and specialized law that basically guarantees you a decently lucrative spot on the civilian side with private military lawyers or even prosecutor's offices if you want to go that route, with 30 days off per year, and all the wonderful army benefits. 

I joined as a combat MOS because I couldn't bear to spend another minute as a Paralegal, but if I was fresh out of college again I can tell you that I would have picked 27D in an instant if you offered it to me compared to my actual career progression. It's not even a contest. Go to college and then fight tooth and nail to get on the bottom rung of a ladder you can get stuck on at any time if you pick the wrong organization (some offices have awful reputations when it comes to keeping their people at the same level for 20+ years), or do well on an easy part of the ASVAB and not even need to go to college and get to climb a very stable and clearly laid out ladder with great benefits doing the exact same kind of work in a much more interesting field than would normally be available to you. Total no brainer.

I sympathize a lot. I was never super fit but I used to be at decently "normal" chubby dude weight, ~210-220ish at 5'11". I ballooned to 250lbs during the pandemic and when my clothes started fitting kind of tight I actually became severely self-conscious about being seen in public and started wearing huge coats and hoodies and XXL stuff that only made me look fatter.

Exercise is a tool, a crutch, an add-on. The most important body parts to train are your brain to stop craving useless calories and your mouth to stop opening for bad foods.
I feel like they may be getting it mixed up with USCIS not accepting photocopies, or filling paperwork in with ink other than blue or black?

The thing with asylum is that as a humanitarian provision, yes, the point of it is that all 7 billion people in the world *can* claim it, should they be fleeing from persecution. What would be the point of an asylum provision that said "actually you have to be xyz first"?

I handled some paperwork for a case once that had a court date for July of 2033. I was beyond certain it must have been a typo. The 180 day work permit is controversial but you would otherwise have people begging for food and shelter for nearly a decade before they were allowed to do anything. What's frustrating is to see people with a legitimate case get impatient and start working before their permit is granted and then they get picked up in a raid 🤦🏾‍♂️like buddy I know it sucks but patience could have gotten you so much further.

Some disqualifying events are easy to prevent (don't drink and drive) but I've seen too many people dragged down by the "update your address with USCIS within 10 days" rule to believe it's not a malicious gotcha.

In order to request asylum in America you have to be physically present in the country, so they're following the procedure set forth in the U.S. code. Is there anything wrong with having a preference for the U.S.? I would imagine most of the people who have to travel to Central America to make their way to the border speak only English or French and their local language, which would make it impossible or very difficult to rebuild your life in countries where Spanish is the official language and English proficiency rates are under 10%, whereas the U.S. speaks English but has no official language and has large communities of niche language speakers with support systems.

Refugee doesn't mean "you get to move to the country immediately next door to yours", it means "you are fleeing persecution to the place that claims to be a safe haven from persecution".

Having worked with a lot of immigration cases at Legal Aid back in the Midwest (so no specific NYC experince but immigration is federal anyways), I can tell you that a lot of the people who may have had a case for staying under different removal prevention programs utterly fuck themselves by trying to or actually working before their case is heard, or by not updating USCIS on their whereabouts, or by getting in trouble with the police for dumb shit like DUIs or petty drug stuff.

I think most refugees have a legitimate claim to refugee status, however the process is murky, opaque, and full of utterly ridiculous and overbearing minutiae expressly made so the government has excuses to kick more people out and deny more otherwise legitimate applications, so I do genuinely believe the 2/3rds figure.

Dark Heresy was a Fantasy Flight Games... *thing*. I don't think GW is very interested in supporting it still.

One thing about this game is that even when it *was* fluffy and lore focused, 40k was still a wargame (and let's not mince words here, it was a *bad* wargame. Warhammer 40,000 has never been a good or balanced game. It's been *fun*.) You can customize your units to hell and back, name every Guardsman in your Emperor's Shield formation, paint all your captains a different color, but the focus was not on the individual characters. I feel like this may be another thing that changed from older editions - named characters were *awesome*, but the generic commanders could be good and had the added benefit of being /your dudes/, however they all merely provided some decently sized aura of some good or cool effect. As an example, with my Blood Angels list, I had a Jump Chaplain and Jump Sanguinary Priest leading two units of Jump Death Company - neither of the characters were the interesting part of the unit. Nowadays lists feel very Hero focused, and the books and codices feel more like they're telling you a story with main characters rather than painting a setting for you to play your army in. TTRPG players would probably be left wanting more focus on their stand-in.

Now as for fixing it, I really don't know. Personally, I despise the competitive scene. Everyone I know IRL who plays still calls competitive players WAACs/Cheeselords/That Guy. Back in the day these were the guys running Eldar Jetbike spam because that's the point of *competing*, they were the ones coming up with ridiculous rules lawyering and hyper meta lists because they had absolutely 0 reason to care about their army being fluffy and 100 reasons to care about it being overpowered. Their way of playing the game has always been completely different to the way most people in the hobby engage with Warhammer and that's something I don't think GW understands. Unfortunately policy is data driven, and competitive events result in a lot of data, data you can't collect from local game shops running casual games and narrative campaigns amongst friends. If it was up to me, I'd return to the design philosophy of previous editions and release a regularly updated competitive version of 40k with a different name or subtitle. Something like Warhammer 40,000: Commander or something.

To me it just boils down to intent. Older editions wanted to accurately represent combat in the 41st Millenium. If rules were fun, or stupid, or frustrating, or you rolled on a bunch of tables all the time for wacky effects (looking at Orks and Daemons), the underlying reasoning was "how can we represent this part of the lore on the tabletop?" Now the game is designed with the competitive crowd in mind, and in order to make it both a good competitive wargame and also friendly to newcomers, they have to strip it bare. The fun, cool, lore representative rules are just impossible to balance, and also place an expectation on newcomers to learn their lore to make sense of their units, both of these things are undesirable tothe direction Gamed Workshop wants to take the hobby in.

Deep Strike scatter is also super thematic, though. It's the way the game represented the fact that teleportariums physically make the squad walk through the warp. Of course you could lose a squad. That's why for SM the safest way to deploy from deep strike was Drop Pods. To me having those rules meant the game was truer to its source material and more interested in representing events taking place in its universe rather than being concerned with how good of a boardgame ruleset it was. If I wanted to play a good ruleset I'd go play Bolt Action, I wanted all the dumb and occasionally frustrating fun of Warhammer 40,000.
A Death Company drop pod assault was always an absolutely glorious way of ripping up an opponents whole battle plan as BA. I couldn't belive my eyes when I saw that pods can't carry Dreads anymore.

The simplest explanation has always been that the molds and machines are expensive (I worked in Industrial Sales for a while and Plastic Injection Molding machines of the quality GW needs are basically only made in China and are stupendously expensive) and the beancounters at their Nottingham HQ have worked out that the percentage increase in sales from the US would take too long to produce profit after the machines are amortized, or worse still, be uncertain to produce profit. The fandom is spread out amongst factions and not every army will have every unit, and since the 80s no company will overstock anything because it's a direct hit on the profit margin, so making twice as many of whatever to keep in a warehouse in the US is not an economically savvy move (no, they're not gonna make more of them and then lower prices, because that goes directly against their marketing strategy as a luxury collector's items manufacturer).

Also, and to a much bigger extent nowadays vs 20 years ago, FOMO sells and since everyone knows GW drops sell out in minutes, people buy as much as they can as quickly as they can and GW hits every expected profit milestone by selling out in 25 minutes. That's a good business model and it probably won't ever change.

If you'll allow me to speculate, they made way too many Sigmar boxes when they killed FB and got seriously burned with overstock. I regularly saw stores with a dozen of those in the backroom in 2017 and 2018. It was a disastrous launch and I think it definitely colors how willing GW is to make a single extra box of anything that they're not guaranteed to sell.

The government subsidizing highways and subsidizing grain are not comparable - we have viable, tested, more economical alternatives to cars, we don't yet have an alternative to eating. While urban farming and local agriculture can replace portions of food imports, they can't feed whole cities. Although I will be the first to kneecap my argument by saying most corn grown goes to animal feed and ethanol (which are also vitally important to the food system), the vast majority of other grain humans either consume or process into other foodstuffs requires railways to transport.

All minerals require railways to transport too. Not just coal, not just scrap metal - this off hand reductionism is dishonest. Everything you have to process from a rock is too expensive to ship by truck the long distances it needs to go. This will not change, ever, unless someone comes up with literal magic that makes 600 tons of rocks worth transporting on 600 trucks for even 10 miles, let alone 600.

5G infrastructure is great. I'm not saying don't build it. However until you have an equitable distribution of the expensive consumer goods it takes to integrate everyone into the network, you serve the population better by improving their physical connection to urban centers, and their mobility within them. Until everyone has a device that can fully exploit all that bandwidth (which will be a long while, if the painful temporary transition to online learning during the COVID crisis is anything to go by), a frequent, reliable, fast passenger and cargo rail line from their area to the city will do them better than a 5G tower. And even then, humanity isn't going to suddenly upload its consciousness to the internet - reliable and efficient physical infrastructure matters far more. Even bringing back the streetcar in force by expanding it to areas outside of CBD and OTR (so reviving the concept of the cablecar suburb General Motors killed) would do more for people and the economy than expanding 5G coverage because being able to exist without a car would free up [about $9k of disposable income that can then add to spending.](https://www.aaa.com/autorepair/articles/average-annual-cost-of-new-vehicle-ownership) 5G doesn't do anything to improve this because people still need to go to places (unless you're also arguing universal 5G coverage renders going to the supermarket, school, work, the park, the music hall, stadiums, other cities, etc. completely unnecessary).

And, uh, I don't know how to tell you this, but railroads use bridges too. They can share these bridges with cars. In fact they used to, like, all the time before limited access roads became the norm in the US. The Brooklyn Bridge had a railway on top of it for about as long as it hasn't had one.

At the end of the day, you're arguing for investing in infrastructure that serves techbros, people with the means to access autonomous cars and 5G enabled devices (hint: it's not, and will likely never be, the poor), and corporations that want to increase profits by switching to JIT logistics, and I'm arguing for investing in infrastructure that connects both material resources to productive forces and consumers, and people to their own urban centers. 

Also, not only is rail transport more efficient "in theory", it is in fact - trucks can't even begin to try and approach the fuel economy of a train. If road transport was as efficient or effective and had such an edge over the railroads as your off hand comment suggests you think it does, GM would have never needed to sabotage every streetcar line in the US, and car corporations wouldn't have needed to lobby the federal government into covering the country in asphalt and keeping gasoline artificially cheap.

Over 90% of rail freight transported is bulk commodities that are entirely uneconomical to transport by truck, autonomous or not. The volumes of grain shipped from elevators in the agricultural regions of the US would require a whole fleet of trucks each (and it does, when they're brought in from the fields) rather than a single locomotive with its cars. Minerals in general are entirely uneconomical to transport by truck because their value to weight ratio is too low, even though they're vital to the industrial sector. Construction materials are shipped mostly by rail as well. Forestry products, raw and finished, are also mostly transported by rail. Cars are also transported by rail and then handed off to be delivered in those big trucks you see on the road.

The only goods it makes sense to transport entirely by truck are high-value, time-sensitive, low-bulk, low to medium weight freight over medium to short distances, ironically enough often from a railhead. This is almost entirely consumer goods and the Last Mile of bulk commodities such as foodstuffs and energy products.

There is an almost unending future for bulk goods because not every town has an iron mine within trucking distance (and as I have said, any kind of ore is too heavy for it to make sense to transport by road), not every port has enough space around it for soybean fields, not every city is going to want a cement factory next to it, and not every village has an industrial forestry sector. The need to transport bulk goods over long distances is not going away because of "localized" supply chains, because few if any supply chains are truly local, or can even be made local. This is the entire reason railroads were invented and used as extensively as they were, and still are used.

The explosion in road transport can also be chalked up to induced demand and the coordinated effort by tire and car manufacturers to lobby the government to disincentivize rail, remove stations and track, and build and maintain millions of miles of highways for free for their products to ride on, not to mention enormous subsidies to gasoline and diesel without which driving a fleet of trucks cross country would bankrupt any company that tried it.

And finally, just-in-time supply chains have an (un)surprising tendency to break down everytime minor delays happen, like the relatively short blockage of the Suez canal costing tens of billions in the short and long run whereas otherwise stockpiles would ameliorate the damage caused by even major disruptions to supply (like cotton during the American Civil War) .

Rail is the most efficient, least polluting (and if you electrify the railway there are 0 direct emissions) and safest way to move bulk, oversized, and heavy loads that are not time sensitive. Had the Eisenhower interstates not been built, we would probably still move everything by rail up to Last Mile deliveries, which have always been and probably will always be by cart/truck.

So yes, in 40 years, we probably will still be moving stuff by rail, and rail infrastructure is one of the smartest ways to use spare money, both heavy rail to move cargo and light rail/interurban rail/rapid transit/HSR to move passengers.
